title: A July pause follows Japan’s rate rise as AI demand enters the inflation outlook
summary: The Bank of Japan left the overnight call-rate guideline at around 1.0% on July 31, following the increase in June. Eight members supported the hold. Hajime Takata proposed another quarter-point rise to 1.25%, arguing that external demand shocks and changes in overseas financial conditions called for a quicker response. The Bank’s simultaneous outlook put numbers on a changing mix of risks. Energy relief lowered its near-term inflation forecast, while global demand for semiconductors, yen depreciation and the prospect of higher domestic wages still threatened more persistent price increases (statement, voting note, and July Outlook, summary).

The fiscal 2026 median forecast for CPI excluding fresh food fell from 2.8% in April to 2.5%. Summer relief on electricity and gas bills was one reason for the revision. The fiscal 2027 median instead rose to 2.4% from 2.3%, with fiscal 2028 steady at 2.0%. For CPI excluding both fresh food and energy, the July medians were 2.5%, 2.6% and 2.2% across those same three years. The lower near-year figure in the main CPI series described a smaller average increase in consumer bills. It gave limited information about the underlying scope for wages or durable-goods prices to rise over subsequent quarters (July Outlook, sections I–II and forecast appendix).

Two different external price channels now mattered. Crude oil affected energy and a range of goods through production and transport costs. Strong global demand for artificial intelligence equipment raised semiconductor and other component prices, while earlier yen depreciation raised the domestic-currency cost of imported items. The Bank expected these forces to become visible in durable goods as well. On the output side, the same AI cycle supported foreign demand and business activity. A stronger technology cycle could thus support Japanese production at the same time that component costs put upward pressure on domestic prices. A broad index of oil-sensitive assets alone would miss that combination (July Outlook, sections II–III).

The Bank judged the risks to economic activity generally balanced, having seen less danger of a large disruption to supply chains than in April. It maintained an upside tilt to price risks. The median real growth forecast was 0.6% in fiscal 2026, 0.8% in fiscal 2027 and 0.8% in fiscal 2028. Household purchasing power still faced pressure from higher import costs, while wage gains, government measures and external demand offered support. Labour shortages, firms’ willingness to pass on cost increases and rising longer-term inflation expectations could keep inflation pressures alive as the direct effect of energy faded. Underlying inflation was expected to reach a target-consistent level between the second half of fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027 (July Outlook, summary and forecast appendix).

The Board also addressed the change in financing conditions after earlier increases. Real rates remained negative mainly over short and medium maturities. In the aggregate, corporate funding costs remained low compared with profitability, with demand for funds increasing and lenders willing to extend credit. This comparison helps interpret the hold. A nominal policy rate of 1.0% gave little information about the restrictiveness facing a firm whose output prices and expected revenues were rising. The same rate could weigh more heavily on a household or smaller importer facing higher bills. The Bank maintained a direction of travel toward further rate increases, conditional on its economic and financial assessment, without specifying the next meeting (July Outlook, section IV).

The rate statement and the Bank’s View appeared at 12:11 Japan time. The information arriving together included Takata’s proposed 1.25% guideline and a lower forecast for current-year consumer inflation. A move in short-dated rates around that minute would measure the market’s response to the package. To distinguish the demand channel from a straightforward change in rate expectations, compare technology exporters with import-intensive domestic sectors and match the yen move against global rates and semiconductor markets. The published statement reports no realized asset returns, and the full outlook text released on August 3 was unavailable during the July event window (statement, release reference).

questions.question: Was the fall in projected fiscal 2026 inflation primarily a summer electricity and gas effect?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the monthly energy contribution using the relief schedule and applicable billing lags. Compare CPI excluding fresh food with the basket excluding both fresh food and energy, then with labour-intensive services. The annual averages can move less than the monthly subsidy effect if part of the reduction later reverses.

questions.question: Did stronger AI demand raise Japanese output, prices or both?
questions.detail: Compare export volumes and receipts for AI-related products with producer and import prices for semiconductors and consumer prices for durables. Separate movements in contract currency from yen-denominated prices and distinguish manufacturers from buyers of components. Those comparisons can reveal who received higher revenues and who faced higher input costs.

questions.question: Did investors treat the July hold as a slower normalization path?
questions.detail: Compare meeting-dated swap repricing at 12:11 with several quarters of forwards, then inspect the yen and relative equity returns. Estimate the policy surprise using expectations captured before publication. A broad rally in global technology assets or a contemporaneous change in foreign rates could produce similar end-of-day patterns without a domestic policy shock.
